title: Curriculum / Content Modifications
description: Modifications that change WHAT the student is taught — the actual curriculum content, mastery level, or scope. Use when the IEP explicitly authorizes content modifications and the student cannot access grade-level material with accommodations alone. Distinct from accommodations: these alter learning expectations and may impact graduation requirements.

source.name: Composite — Wikipedia (IEP, Special Education)
source.section: Modifications, Specially designed instruction, IEP components

modifications.text: Skip curriculum sections that the IEP team deems inappropriate or out-of-reach for the student. Example: a student with poor fine motor skills may be taught printed letters but not cursive handwriting; another student may focus on identifying hours while the class learns minutes.

Substitute a lower-grade-level version of the same conceptual material. Example: a student in 6th grade reading at a 2nd-grade level may use a 2nd-grade-level retelling of a literary work the class is studying, while still participating in class discussion about the themes.

Use parallel texts with both the original and a modern paraphrase available (e.g., side-by-side Shakespeare). The student engages with the simpler version while the class engages with the original. Discussion of meaning, themes, and author's craft can still be shared.

Modify the learning objectives for a lesson or unit so the student is expected to master a subset of skills rather than all skills. Example: while the class is mastering vocabulary AND spelling AND grammatical use of new words, the modified objective is mastery of meaning only.

When the student's IEP indicates a foundational skill gap, substitute targeted prerequisite instruction during a portion of the lesson. Example: while peers do multi-step word problems, a student working on integer rules continues that focused work with a special-education teacher push-in or pull-out.

Present curriculum content through multiple modalities (visual, auditory, kinesthetic) where the student's disability impedes single-modality access. Example: when the class reads a content-area text, the student receives the same content via teacher-narration, audio recording, video, AND text.

Apply a 'focused grade' — a grade that is recognized in a high school diploma but is annotated as 'focused' to indicate the student met modified mastery criteria. Use only when authorized by the IEP team and consistent with state graduation rules.

guardrails.text: Only apply modifications that the IEP explicitly authorizes in its Modifications section. Generating modifications beyond IEP authorization is outside the scope of any single-lesson modification request — flag instead.
In high school grades, content modifications may impact graduation eligibility. Always check the IEP's Schedule Modification and Assessment sections before recommending broad content modifications.
Prefer accommodations over modifications wherever possible. Modify only when the student cannot meaningfully access the content with accommodations alone.
